title: Lunch That Does Not Cost You the Afternoon

cards.title: The 3pm Crash Is a Lunch Problem
cards.content:
You know the feeling. Somewhere between two and four in the afternoon the room gets heavy, the screen stops making sense, and you go looking for biscuits. Most people treat that as an afternoon problem and reach for an afternoon solution: coffee, sugar, a walk to the machine.

It is a **lunch** problem. The standard desk lunch **sandwich, crisps and a sweet drink** is close to a pure refined-carbohydrate load: fast starch, fast sugar, very little protein, very little fibre, almost no fat worth the name. Your 3:00 was decided at 12:30.

This lesson is not about willpower and it is not about giving up sandwiches. It is about a repeatable way to put a decent lunch in front of yourself in under six minutes on a working day.

cards.title: Lunch Is Assembly, Not Cookery
cards.content:
Here is the rule that makes weekday lunch work: **lunch is assembled, not cooked.** If a lunch requires cooking on a Tuesday, it will not happen on a Tuesday. You will be busy, or late, or on a call, and the meal deal will win.

So stop looking for lunch recipes. Recipes are for evenings and weekends. What you need at midday is a **template with four slots** and a fridge stocked so the slots can be filled without a decision.

This is exactly the Permanent Plate logic applied to the meal you are most likely to outsource: half the container plants of varied colour, a palm of protein, a fist of intact starch if you want it, a thumb of extra-virgin olive oil, and something fermented most days.

The cooking, where there is any, happens the night before or on a Sunday. Midday is tipping things into a bowl.

cards.title: The Four-Part Assembly
cards.content:
Every lunch in this lesson is the same four slots in the same order.

1. **Base**: two big handfuls of leaves, or a fist of intact grain such as barley, quinoa, brown rice or a slice of dense rye. Not both unless you are hungry.

2. **Protein**: a palm. Tinned salmon, mackerel or sardines, two boiled eggs, last night's chicken, a half-tin of beans or chickpeas, feta, cottage cheese.

3. **At least two colours of vegetable**: cucumber and tomato, roasted carrot and red pepper, grated carrot and red cabbage. Two is the minimum, not the target.

4. **Dressing**: built on **extra-virgin olive oil**. This is the slot people skip, and it is the slot that decides whether you eat the thing.

Fill the four slots and you have lunch. There is nothing else to remember.

cards.title: The Jar of Dressing
cards.content:
A proper vinaigrette is roughly **three parts extra-virgin olive oil to one part acid**, with mustard as the emulsifier and enough salt to taste. That is the whole thing.

In a jam jar: **6 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil**, **2 tbsp red wine vinegar** or lemon juice, **1 tsp Dijon mustard**, **one small crushed garlic clove**, salt and black pepper. Lid on, shake hard for fifteen seconds until it goes thick and creamy. It keeps about two weeks in the fridge, and it will separate; shake it again before each use.

The mustard is not a flavour note, it is the mechanic. It holds the oil and acid together so the dressing coats the leaves instead of sliding off into the bottom of the box.

A jar of this in the fridge removes the single biggest excuse for a dull salad. Adjust the acid to taste; some vinegars are sharper than others, so start at 3 to 1 and go from there.

cards.title: Do This: Make a Jar This Week
cards.content:
This is the highest-leverage six minutes in the whole lesson. Do it once and eight lunches get better.

1. **Buy five things**: a decent extra-virgin olive oil, red wine vinegar, Dijon mustard, lemons, and a jam jar with a tight lid. All five live in the cupboard from now on.

2. **Make it tonight**: oil and acid in the jar at 3 to 1, then mustard, garlic, salt and pepper. Shake for fifteen seconds.

3. **Put it in the front row of the fridge door**, not the back of a shelf. If you cannot see it, you will not use it.

4. **Use it on something within 24 hours** so the habit attaches to a real meal, even if that is just leaves alongside tonight's dinner.

If you want a second jar, make the tahini version from later in this lesson. Two dressings is enough variety for a working week.

cards.title: Build 1: The Big Bowl
cards.content:
The default. No heat, no chopping board if you are in a hurry, four minutes start to finish.

• **Two big handfuls of salad leaves** in the bottom of a bowl or a large box
• **One tin of salmon or mackerel**, drained, flaked over the top
• **Half a tin of chickpeas**, rinsed
• **Half a cucumber**, chunked, and **six cherry tomatoes**, halved
• **A quarter of a red onion**, sliced as thin as you can
• **Two tablespoons of the dressing**, added last

Toss it with your hands, which coats things far better than a fork does. Eat the vegetables and the fish before you touch any bread you have with it.

One note on timing: if this is travelling to work, keep the dressing separate and add it at your desk. Leaves dressed at 8am are soup by 1pm.

cards.title: Build 2: Leftovers-Plus
cards.content:
The cheapest lunch you will ever make, because you already cooked it.

The move is at **dinner**, not at lunch: cook two extra portions and box one **before you sit down to eat**. Food that is boxed while you are still standing at the hob actually makes it to the fridge. Food you plan to box afterwards gets picked at.

At 12:30 the next day, the box is not lunch on its own; it is a component. Add:

• **Two handfuls of leaves**, dressed
• **A tablespoon of sauerkraut or kimchi** on the side
• **A spoon of dressing** over the whole thing

That is roast chicken and vegetables turned into a full plate in ninety seconds. The leaves and the ferment are doing the work; without them it is a reheat, with them it is a meal that hits plants, protein, fat and fibre.

Eat cooked leftovers within about three days, and reheat properly hot if you are heating them at all.

cards.question: It is 12:30 on a Tuesday. In the fridge: a bag of salad leaves, a tin of mackerel, half a tin of chickpeas and a jar of olive oil dressing. No hob, four minutes. What is the best move?

options.text: Leave it, buy a baguette meal deal now, and use the fridge food at the weekend when there is time to cook properly
Leaves in the bowl, mackerel and chickpeas on top, two tablespoons of dressing, toss with your hands and eat
Eat the mackerel and chickpeas on their own and skip the leaves, since the protein and fat are what actually matter
Assemble and dress the whole thing at 8am so it is ready and waiting when you get hungry

cards.explanation: Those four items are already the full assembly: base, protein, two vegetables if you count the chickpeas, and a dressing. It needs no cooking. The tempting wrong answer is dressing it at 8am, which sounds organised but is not: dressed leaves collapse within a couple of hours, and a limp box is the fastest route back to the meal deal. Keep the dressing separate and add it at the desk.

cards.title: Build 3: Soup, Leaves and Rye
cards.content:
For cold days, and for anyone who does not want a salad in January.

**The batch, Sunday, about 40 minutes:** soften a chopped onion, two carrots and two sticks of celery in **two tablespoons of olive oil**. Add **200g red lentils**, a **tin of chopped tomatoes**, **1.2 litres of stock**, a teaspoon of cumin and a bay leaf. Simmer 25 minutes until the lentils are completely soft. Blitz half of it so it is thick but still has texture. Cool and box into four portions.

**The lunch:** a big mugful of soup, plus **a handful of dressed leaves**, plus **one slice of dense rye** with a thumb of butter or olive oil. A spoon of sauerkraut on the side if you have it, fruit after.

Soup alone is not lunch; it empties fast and you are hunting biscuits by three. Soup plus leaves plus rye is a whole plate. Keeps four days in the fridge, or freeze two portions on the day you make it.

cards.title: Build 4: The Grain Bowl
cards.content:
When you want something more substantial than leaves.

• **Base**: a fist of cooked **pearl barley** or **quinoa**, cooked in a batch and cooled. Barley takes about 30 minutes, quinoa about 15.
• **Vegetables**: a big handful of **roasted vegetables**, two colours minimum. Roast a whole tray at once: carrots, red peppers, red onion, courgette, tossed in olive oil at 200C for 30 to 35 minutes.
• **Protein**: a palm of **feta**, or **chickpeas**, or both.
• **Dressing**: **tahini** rather than vinaigrette, for variety.

**Tahini dressing:** 2 tbsp tahini, the juice of half a lemon, a pinch of salt, a little crushed garlic, then warm water a teaspoon at a time until it goes from seized and stiff to pourable. It will look wrong before it looks right; keep adding water.

A handful of chopped parsley or mint on top counts toward your 30 plants and makes the whole bowl taste less like leftovers.

cards.title: Build 5: The Genuinely Bought Lunch
cards.content:
Some days you are buying lunch. That is not a failure and it does not need pretending otherwise. It needs a decision rule: **build the best version available from what is actually in front of you.**

At a supermarket meal deal:

• **Main**: a chicken or tuna salad box, or a wholegrain sandwich with visible protein, instead of a white baguette
• **Side**: a bag of leaves, a side salad, edamame, or a boiled egg pot instead of crisps
• **Drink**: water or unsweetened coffee, and keep the fruit or nuts for after

In a canteen: start at the vegetables, take two colours, add the protein dish, and treat the starch as the third thing on the plate rather than the base of it. If there is oil and vinegar on the table, use it.

If the only real option is a sandwich, take it, eat the side salad first, and take the ten-minute walk afterwards. A bought lunch built deliberately beats a home lunch you did not make.

cards.title: The Sad Desk Salad, Diagnosed
cards.content:
Most people who say they do not like salad have only ever eaten a bad one: naked leaves, cold plain chicken, a few tomatoes, no dressing. That is not a meal, it is a punishment, and nobody sustains a punishment.

Vegetables become genuinely enjoyable when four things are present. Miss one and the bowl reads as a chore.

• **Salt**: season the vegetables themselves, not just the dressing. A pinch of flaky salt on tomatoes and cucumber changes them completely.
• **Acid**: lemon or vinegar in the dressing, plus a second squeeze at the desk if it tastes flat.
• **Fat**: olive oil, avocado, feta, olives, toasted seeds. Fat carries flavour and it is why the dressing slot exists.
• **Texture**: something crunchy and something soft in every bowl. Toasted seeds, nuts, croutons of rye, raw fennel against soft egg or avocado.

If a salad tastes boring, run the four levers before you conclude you do not like salad. It is almost always missing acid or salt.

cards.explanation: The vinaigrette delivers three of the four levers in one move: fat from the olive oil, acid from the vinegar, and salt. That is why the jar earns its shelf space. cards.title: What Survives Three Days in the Fridge
cards.content:
Batching works only if you batch the right things. The rule is simple: **batch the sturdy components, add the fragile ones on the day.**

**Keeps three days or more:** cooked barley, quinoa and rice; roasted root vegetables and squash; cooked lentils and beans; boiled eggs left in the shell; undressed chopped cabbage, carrot and fennel; feta, olives and tinned fish; the jar of dressing. Soup keeps about four days, or freeze it.

**Does not:** dressed leaves, which wilt within hours; cut avocado, which is a same-day item even with lemon on it; sliced tomato, which floods a box; anything crunchy once it is sitting in liquid. Cooked fish is a two-day item.

So the box that works is: sturdy things layered in, wet and fragile things carried separately, dressing in a small pot or waiting at work. Assemble at the last minute.

Cool cooked food quickly before it goes in the fridge, and keep it in the fridge rather than in a bag under a warm desk.

cards.title: Do This: Build Tomorrow Lunch Tonight
cards.content:
Ten minutes tonight, while dinner is cooking, removes tomorrow's decision entirely.

1. **Box the leftovers before you sit down.** Not after. Portion straight from the pan into a lidded box and put it in the fridge while you eat.

2. **Fill a second box** with the base and vegetables: leaves, or grain and roasted veg, or chopped cucumber, tomato and cabbage. Undressed.

3. **A small pot of dressing**, or keep a jar in the fridge at work if there is one.

4. **Fruit and a small handful of nuts** into the bag by the door, not left in the kitchen drawer where you will forget them.

Tomorrow at 12:30 you make no decisions at all. That is the whole point: the choice is made at 9pm by a version of you who is not hungry, not rushed, and not standing in a queue.

Do it for three days this week. Not seven. Three is a habit, seven is a project.

cards.title: When You Cannot Eat It In Order
cards.content:
The first rule of this programme is to eat in order: vegetables and protein before starch. That works beautifully with an assembled lunch, where the components sit separately on the plate and you simply start with the vegetables.

A sandwich defeats it. A wrap, a burrito, a pasta salad and a filled roll are all **single mixed objects** with the starch woven through them. There is no order to eat them in.

When you cannot sequence the meal, pull the other lever: **a ten to fifteen minute walk immediately after eating.** Contracting muscle pulls glucose out of the blood through contraction-mediated GLUT4 translocation, which does not require insulin at all. It is the highest return per unit of effort anywhere in this programme, and it works on a sandwich day.

The timing matters. The walk goes straight after lunch, not at 3pm when the slump has already arrived.

**Important:** if you take insulin or a sulfonylurea, adding walks alongside these diet changes lowers glucose further and can cause a hypo. Talk to your doctor or diabetes nurse about dose adjustment before you start.

cards.title: Do This: Fix Your Usual Lunch
cards.content:
This exercise is deliberately not about replacing what you eat. Most lunch plans fail because they ask you to abandon a habit; this one modifies it.

1. **Write down what you actually eat at lunch**, most days, honestly. Not what you intend to eat.

2. **Add a plant course before it.** A bag of leaves with dressing, a side salad, a tub of chopped cucumber and pepper. Eat that first, then the usual lunch.

3. **Add a protein.** A boiled egg, a small tin of tuna, a pot of cottage cheese or a handful of nuts alongside.

4. **Swap the drink**, if it is a sweet one, for water, and keep fruit for after rather than instead.

Worked example: cheese sandwich, crisps and a fizzy drink becomes leaves with dressing, then a boiled egg, then the sandwich, water, and an apple afterwards. The sandwich is still there. Nothing was banned and nothing was earned; the shape of the meal simply changed.

Run this for a week before you try any of the five builds. If the additions stick, the builds are easy.

cards.question: You are batching lunch components on Sunday for the week ahead. Which of these will still be genuinely good on Wednesday?

options.text: A big tub of leaves tossed with dressing on Sunday morning
Sliced avocado in a sealed tub with a squeeze of lemon on it
Pearl barley, boiled, drained, cooled and boxed plain
Tomatoes sliced and salted on Sunday, stacked in a tub

cards.explanation: Cooked grain is the sturdiest thing in the list: cooled and boxed undressed, barley holds up for three or four days and gives you a base to build on. Dressed leaves are the tempting wrong answer because the work feels efficiently done, but salt and acid draw water out of the leaves within hours and by Wednesday it is a wet bag. Avocado browns the same day, and salted tomatoes flood the box.
